stingray.title: THIS FISH FLIES UNDERWATER
stingray.script: A stingray seems to fly underwater because its broad pectoral fins move like wings. Rays are close relatives of sharks, so their skeletons are made of flexible cartilage instead of bone. Many species cruise near the seafloor and can detect faint electrical signals from prey hidden in sand. Their eyes sit on top of the body while the mouth and gill openings are underneath. Some stingrays bury themselves almost completely for camouflage. The tail spine is mainly defensive, not a hunting weapon, and most rays prefer escaping to fighting.
stingray.caption:
Stingrays glide through water like underwater wings. 🌊

dolphin.title: DOLPHINS CAN SEE WITH SOUND
dolphin.script: Dolphins can build a picture of the world using sound. They send out rapid clicks and listen for echoes returning from fish, rocks, and the seafloor. Those echoes reveal distance, direction, shape, and movement. This biological sonar is called echolocation, and it helps dolphins hunt even when the water is dark or cloudy. Dolphins also breathe consciously through a blowhole, so surfacing is an active behavior. They are highly social, coordinate with their pod, and use whistles and clicks to stay in contact while swimming or hunting.
dolphin.caption:
Dolphins can map their surroundings with echoes. 🐬

crab.title: WHY CRABS WALK SIDEWAYS
crab.script: Many crabs move sideways because their leg joints make lateral motion faster and more stable than walking straight ahead. That body plan helps them cross sand, rocks, and shallow seafloors without turning first. A crab wears a hard exoskeleton on the outside, but the shell cannot stretch as the animal grows. So it has to molt. The old shell splits, the crab pulls free, and the new shell stays soft until it hardens. Some species can also regrow a missing leg or claw over later molts.
crab.caption:
Crabs are built for sideways speed. 🦀
